facts.text: Coker Creek was Cherokee land before removal in 1838 and was called 'Coco' or 'Coqua,' the Cherokee name for butterfly weed.
Europeans learned of placer gold in the area, and from 1827 illegal mining by Peck and Henderson sparked a rush that continued until 1911.
A trading path between lower settlements and overhill towns passed through Coker Creek, becoming the Unicoi Turnpike in 1816.
General Walker Keith Armistead built Fort Armistead at Meroney's Stand to repel prospectors, later serving as a waypoint during the Cherokee removal.
Coker Creek lies in the southern Appalachian Mountains, surrounded by Cherokee National Forest just west of the Tennessee‑North Carolina line.
The Coker Creek Heritage Group, a non‑profit, preserves the community’s rich heritage and history.
